messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 59
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Professor
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 54

Dr. Mensah is a 59-year-old professor of African literature at a large public university. He has been single for over a decade, living alone in a modest apartment near campus. Five years ago, during a summer research trip to the coast of Ghana, he took his only daughter, twenty-five-year-old Amara, to a secluded beach near Cape Coast. The water was calm, and she was an experienced swimmer. He watched from the shore as she waded out, then saw her suddenly struggle. He ran into the water, but the rip current was too strong. By the time he reached her, she was unconscious. He carried her body to the sand and performed CPR until help arrived. She never regained consciousness. The paramedics said she likely died within the first two minutes.

Now, in his office, Dr. Mensah keeps the door slightly ajar—a habit he cannot explain, because he always closes it to grade papers. He cannot tolerate the sound of water running in the sink, so he uses hand sanitizer constantly. His colleagues have noticed he avoids the campus lake and will not attend any department event held near a pool or fountain. He stopped teaching his popular course on maritime literature because every line about the sea pulled him back to that afternoon. Instead, he now teaches only seminars on inland epics, novels set in deserts and mountains. When students ask about the symbolism of water in a text, he changes the subject or deflects with a dry remark.

At night, he dreams of Amara standing on a beach, her back turned. He calls out, but she does not hear. Then the water rises slowly, and he cannot move his feet. He wakes with his heart pounding, drenched in sweat, and lies in the dark for an hour, replaying the moment he first saw her arm go under. He has not visited a beach or a pool in five years. He cannot even tolerate the sound of a shower; he takes baths, but only after covering his ears with a towel.

During faculty meetings, his mind drifts. He sees Amara’s face when he told her the itinerary, the way she smiled and said, “I’ve always wanted to see the slave castles with you.” Now he avoids any mention of Ghana in his lectures. When a colleague once praised his work on oral traditions from the coast, he excused himself and spent the next hour in the restroom, staring at the floor. He has not replied to invitations from his brother in Accra for three years. He feels a heavy guilt, convinced that if he had been a stronger swimmer, if he had not insisted on that beach, she would be alive. His students notice he sometimes pauses mid-sentence, his eyes unfocused, and then resumes as if nothing happened.

He canceled all travel plans indefinitely. The last time he flew was to attend his daughter’s memorial, and the plane’s descent over the ocean triggered a full-blown panic attack. Since then, he takes trains or stays put. His office walls are bare except for a single photograph of Amara as a child, turned facing the wall. When a well-meaning student gave him a seashell as a gift, he thanked her stiffly and later threw it away in the department dumpster. There are days when his mind returns to the beach without warning—while he is lecturing on Yoruba proverbs or reading a student’s essay on identity. He continues grading, but his hands tremble. He repeats to himself that it was an accident, but the words feel hollow. At night, he sometimes dials Amara’s old phone number just to hear the disconnected tone, then hangs up without leaving a message. He tells no one about this ritual.
